candidate_relations.reason: The inferomedial intraconal mass has intrinsic melanin-like T1 hyperintensity and T2 hypointensity rather than a lesion arising from an optic nerve sheath or dura.
No continuity with an orbital nerve is reported, and the signal pattern is dominated by paramagnetic pigment or blood products.
Six months of steady proptosis and a well-defined solid-appearing mass with bone scalloping do not show the positional enlargement expected for an orbital varix.
Intact motility, absence of pain or optic signs, and a sharply circumscribed intraconal mass argue against idiopathic orbital inflammation.
Orbital tumor correctly localizes the lesion but provides no melanocytic identity or benign melanocytoma behavior.
Cavernous hemangioma can be intraconal and circumscribed, but the marked T1-high and T2-low signal is more consistent with a melanotic lesion.
Systemic metastatic evaluation is negative and the solitary slow-growing lesion has no evidence establishing metastatic malignancy.
The remote right choroidal melanoma makes metastasis a major differential, but no systemic disease or biopsy evidence supports metastatic spread to the left orbit.
The intraconal location and displacement are compatible with cavernous hemangioma, yet the melanin-like MRI signal and intrinsic dense foci point to a different tissue type.
A negative metastatic survey and isolated left orbital mass do not justify replacing a primary benign melanocytic diagnosis with metastasis.
Prior choroidal melanoma is clinically relevant, but the record gives no recurrence, systemic lesions, or pathology linking this mass to that primary.
The T1-bright and T2-dark lesion suggests pigment, whereas no fibrous histology or characteristic enhancement establishes solitary fibrous tumor.
Contralateral orbital metastasis from the 2010 melanoma remains possible but is not demonstrated by the negative workup or pre-biopsy imaging record.
The lesion is described as a discrete intraconal mass causing progressive proptosis, not a network of abnormal orbital vessels.
Normal anterior and posterior segment examinations and lack of ocular pain do not support scleritis.
A small solitary pigmented-signal intraconal lesion without systemic lymphadenopathy is not characteristic of lymphoma.
The known choroidal melanoma was in the enucleated right eye, while this lesion is a left intraconal orbital mass with no intraocular origin.
Progression without inflammatory pain, restricted motility, or optic neuropathy and the sharply bounded mass morphology oppose inflammatory orbital disease.
There is no scleral primary or biopsy evidence of metastasis, and the prior malignancy originated in the contralateral choroid.
The imaging phenotype may mimic melanoma metastasis, but negative systemic staging and absent histology leave that malignant origin unsupported.

case_quality_flags: The record ends before incisional-biopsy histopathology, so melanocytoma cannot be securely distinguished from melanoma metastasis or other pigmented orbital tumors.
